WalkthroughText: Two boolean expressions are equivalent if they produce the exact same true/false result for every possible combination of their variables' values — you can verify this by checking a truth table row by row. De Morgan's laws give us a reliable way to rewrite negated compound expressions: !(A && B) is always equivalent to !A || !B, and !(B || A) is always equivalent to !A && !B. Notice the pattern — negating flips '&&' to '||' (and vice versa) AND negates each individual piece inside. We'll use the boolTruthGlow visualization to watch two expressions light up in identical patterns across all four true/false combinations of two variables, proving they're equivalent.

PracticeItems.Prompt: Which expression is equivalent to !(a > 5 && b < 10) using De Morgan's laws?
PracticeItems.Explanation: De Morgan's law states !(P && Q) is equivalent to !P || !Q. Negating '&&' flips it to '||', and each condition is negated: a > 5 becomes a <= 5, and b < 10 becomes b >= 10. The second choice keeps '&&' instead of switching to '||', which is the classic De Morgan mistake. The third and fourth choices fail to negate one or both of the inner conditions.

PracticeItems.Prompt: Which expression is equivalent to !(x == 0 || y == 0)?
PracticeItems.Explanation: De Morgan's law states !(P || Q) is equivalent to !P && !Q. So '||' becomes '&&', and each equality is negated to become an inequality. The second choice incorrectly keeps '||' instead of switching to '&&'. The fourth choice only negates one of the two conditions, so it is not fully equivalent.

PracticeItems.Prompt: A boolean expression is tested for all four combinations of true/false values of its two variables p and q, and it glows true in exactly the same rows as (p && q). Which of the following expressions must produce that same truth pattern?
PracticeItems.Explanation: By De Morgan's law, !(!p || !q) simplifies to p && q, which matches the required truth pattern exactly (true only when both p and q are true). The choice '!p || !q' is actually the negation of p && q, so it glows true in the opposite rows. 'p || q' is true whenever at least one is true, which glows true in more rows than p && q. '!(p && !q)' simplifies to !p || q, which does not match either.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Let's compare two expressions: !(p && q) and !p || !q. We'll test them against every combination of p and q to see if they always agree.
Row 1: p is true, q is true. First let's evaluate p && q, which is true, so !(p && q) becomes false.
Now check !p || !q for the same row: !p is false and !q is false, so false || false is also false. They match!
Row 2: p is true, q is false. p && q is false, so !(p && q) becomes true.
Check !p || !q here: !p is false, !q is true, so false || true is true. Still matching.
Row 3: p is false, q is true. p && q is false, so !(p && q) is true.
Check !p || !q: !p is true, !q is false, so true || false is true. Matches again.
Row 4: p is false, q is false. p && q is false, so !(p && q) is true.
Check !p || !q: !p is true, !q is true, so true || true is true. They match on all four rows, so !(p && q) is truly equivalent to !p || !q — this is De Morgan's law in action.
